Basis. A minimal set of linearly independent vectors that span an entire vector space. A basis for a vector space is a set of vectors that are linearly independent—no nontrivial linear combination equals zero—and span the space, meaning every vector is a linear combination of basis vectors. Every vector in the space can be uniquely expressed as a linear combination of basis vectors.

The dimension of a vector space is the cardinality of any basis, a fundamental invariant. All bases of the same space have equal size, making dimension well-defined. The standard basis for R to the n is the unit vectors along coordinate axes; any vector has a unique representation as a linear combination of these basis vectors. Change of basis occurs via a transition matrix P, where coordinates transform; this is useful when a non-standard basis simplifies a problem, such as an eigenvector basis that diagonalizes a matrix.

Orthonormal bases consist of mutually perpendicular unit vectors, like the standard basis. They enable simple computations: dot products and projections become scalar multiplications. The Gram-Schmidt method constructs such bases. A linear transformation from vector space V to W is represented by a matrix whose columns are the images of basis vectors of V. Different basis choices yield different matrices for the same transformation.

The rank of a matrix is the dimension of its image. The rank-nullity theorem states that rank plus nullity equals the number of columns, and full rank means the transformation is injective. Hamel bases exist for any vector space by the axiom of choice, but infinite-dimensional spaces require uncountably many basis vectors, making Hamel bases impractical for analysis. Schauder bases and frame theory provide practical alternatives for infinite-dimensional spaces like Hilbert and Banach spaces, enabling convergent expansions even when not every vector is a finite combination.
